nameStory: The Waved Sphinx gets its name from the wavy, undulating lines that ripple across its forewings like gentle waves on water. This moth is also called the 'Scorpion Moth' because its caterpillar rears up its front end when threatened, arching like a scorpion ready to strike – though it's completely harmless!
description: The Waved Sphinx is a large, robust moth with a wingspan that can reach 4-5 inches across. Its forewings display beautiful wavy patterns in shades of gray, brown, and cream that create excellent camouflage against tree bark. Like all sphinx moths, it has a thick, streamlined body and narrow wings that make it a powerful flier. During the day, it rests with its wings folded back, looking remarkably like a piece of bark or a broken twig.

idTips.label: Wavy wing pattern
idTips.description: Look for the distinctive zigzag or wavy lines running across the gray-brown forewings – they feel smooth to the touch and shimmer slightly in the light

idTips.label: Large size
idTips.description: This is a hefty moth with a thick, fuzzy body about as wide as your thumb and wings that span your whole hand

idTips.label: Bark-like coloration
idTips.description: Mottled grays and browns that blend perfectly with tree bark, often with subtle cream or tan highlights

idTips.label: Streamlined body
idTips.description: Dense, soft fur covers a torpedo-shaped body that tapers to a pointed tip – feels like velvet when gently touched

idTips.label: Resting position
idTips.description: Wings fold back along the body like a fighter jet, with the moth pressed tight against vertical surfaces

habitat: Waved Sphinx moths are found throughout New England's deciduous and mixed forests, especially where ash trees grow since that's what their caterpillars prefer to eat. Look for adults around porch lights, gas stations, and other bright lights at night during summer months. They're also attracted to night-blooming flowers like honeysuckle and moonflowers in suburban gardens and forest edges.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late May, with the first generation appearing as temperatures warm and ash trees leaf out.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity occurs in June and July when adults are most commonly seen at lights. A second generation may appear in late summer.
seasonality.fall: Adult activity winds down in early fall, though some late stragglers may be seen into September on warm nights.
seasonality.winter: Pupae overwinter buried in soil at the base of host trees, completely dormant until spring warmth triggers emergence.

funFact: When the Waved Sphinx caterpillar feels threatened, it can actually make a clicking sound by rapidly opening and closing its jaws – one of the few moth caterpillars that's truly 'vocal' and can be heard from several feet away!
confusionNotes: The Waved Sphinx is most easily confused with other large gray sphinx moths, but remember the waves – those distinctive wavy lines across the forewings are your best clue. Other sphinx moths tend to have straighter lines, spots, or different patterns entirely.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called the 'Scorpion Moth,' this species is completely harmless to humans. The scorpion comparison only applies to the defensive posture of the caterpillar, which has no stinger or ability to harm anything larger than the ash leaves it munches on.
compareHints: As the only Ceratomia species commonly found in New England, the Waved Sphinx is most similar to other large sphinx moths like the Big Poplar Sphinx or Modest Sphinx. However, those species lack the distinctive wavy wing patterns and tend to be more uniformly colored. The Waved Sphinx's combination of size, wavy markings, and gray-brown bark camouflage makes it fairly distinctive among our regional sphinx moths.
